extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of communication/media studies; journalists or researchers learning Entman's framing model
extracted.subtask_description: Explain and apply Robert Entman's four framing functions—problem definition, causal interpretation, moral evaluation, and treatment recommendation—to analyze how media and communicators construct and influence public understanding of issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem Definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of identifying and highlighting a specific issue or event as a problem worthy of attention (Entman, 1993).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Involves selecting aspects of a perceived reality and making them more salient in a communicating text. Example: in reporting on climate change, emphasising rising global temperatures and extreme weather frames the issue as an urgent crisis. Problem definition is a strategic choice that sets the public agenda and can overshadow alternative perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal Interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributing responsibility for the defined problem (Entman, 1993).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies causes or origins of the issue and thereby influences perceptions of accountability. Example: framing economic inequality as caused by government policies versus corporate greed leads audiences to different conclusions about who is responsible. Causal interpretation often reveals underlying biases in communication because different causal frames produce contrasting interpretations of the same issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Making ethical judgments about the problem and its causes (Entman, 1993).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses moral implications by invoking values or principles to evaluate actions of individuals or institutions. Example: immigration discourse framed as humane versus unjust. Moral evaluation frequently appeals to emotions and can polarise opinions by presenting issues in terms of right or wrong, thus shaping audience alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment Recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggesting remedies or actions to address the defined problem (Entman, 1993).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposes solutions or policy responses that guide audiences toward particular courses of action. Example: in a public health frame, recommending taxes on sugary drinks versus promoting individual lifestyle changes. Treatment recommendations are inherently persuasive but can oversimplify complex issues and limit the range of considered options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations: oversimplification and bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Framing choices can introduce bias and risk oversimplifying complex issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The framework warns that selective emphasis and causal attributions are not neutral and may obscure alternative perspectives or underlying complexities. When evaluating or producing frames, consider whether the frame unfairly narrows discussion, marginalises other explanations, or manipulates emotional responses.
